questions.q: Why does this lesson say the Username-Password OAuth flow is a poor fit for new integrations?
options: It requires the integration to hold the user's actual password, duplicating that secret and tying authentication to rules designed for a human login, not a service
It is the fastest of all OAuth flows and therefore unsuitable for slow networks
Salesforce has completely removed the ability to use it in any org
It can only be used by mobile apps, never by server-to-server integrations
questions.explain: Username-Password ties authentication to a real password that now exists in two places and inherits human-oriented password rules -- current guidance favors flows built for machine use instead.

questions.q: What makes the JWT Bearer flow a good fit for an unattended, no-UI server-to-server integration?
options: It requires a browser login every time a token is needed
It authenticates with a signed token validated against an uploaded certificate, with no browser or human interaction needed at request time
It is the only flow that supports refresh tokens
It bypasses all permission checks on the Salesforce side
questions.explain: JWT Bearer signs a JSON Web Token with a private key and exchanges it directly for an access token -- no browser, no login screen, which is exactly what a scheduled unattended job needs.

questions.q: In the Client Credentials flow, what determines everything the integration is allowed to do once it has a token?
options: The permissions of the connected app's configured 'Run As' user
The strength of the client secret used to request the token
The number of API calls made in the prior 24 hours
The browser the request originated from
questions.explain: Client Credentials runs every call as a specific pre-configured Run As user, so that user's profile and permission sets are the real boundary on what the integration can do -- the flow itself only proves identity, not authorization scope.

questions.q: A multi-tenant SaaS product needs each of its customers to individually connect their own separate Salesforce org and explicitly consent before the app can access their data. Which OAuth flow fits this requirement, per this lesson?
options: Client Credentials flow
JWT Bearer flow
Authorization Code flow
There is no OAuth flow that supports this use case
questions.explain: Authorization Code flow is built around a human logging in through a browser and explicitly consenting -- exactly the per-customer consent model a multi-tenant product needs, unlike the unattended Client Credentials or JWT Bearer flows.

questions.q: This lesson argues that choosing an OAuth flow and scoping the identity behind it are two separate decisions. What example does it give to illustrate this?
options: A perfectly configured JWT Bearer setup pointed at a System Administrator user is still a dangerously over-privileged integration
OAuth flows automatically scope themselves to the minimum permissions needed
Client Credentials flow cannot be pointed at any user with administrative rights
Choosing a flow is impossible without first creating a permission set
questions.explain: The OAuth flow only governs how the integration proves its identity -- it says nothing about what that identity is allowed to do. A JWT Bearer flow pointed at an over-privileged user is just as risky as any other integration with that same user behind it.
